title: The sisters' songs, one
hookLine: read the short poems of the Therigatha's first chapters
tomorrow: she lost everyone she loved. how did she end up teaching?

cards: Somewhere a stone pestle is coming down into a stone mortar, crushing garlic or lemongrass or spice. Some kitchens still make that sound every day, and for a woman named Mutta it was the sound of her whole life.
Her poem, in the Therigatha, is a single breath of relief. In plain paraphrase: freed, so freed, from three crooked things. The mortar.
The pestle. And my crooked husband. Free from birth and death too; what pulled me back to them is gone.

teach.h: POEMS SPOKEN BY THE ELDER SISTERS.
teach.b: The Therigatha is a collection in the Pali Canon of poems spoken by early Buddhist nuns, the elder sisters. The first chapters are tiny, one or two verses each, and they're full of things you can touch.
The very first is spoken to an unnamed nun: sleep softly, little sister, wrapped in a robe you sewed from rags.
Your wanting has gone quiet, like herbs dried in a pot. Smell that for a second. Not a symbol from a temple, but a jar on a kitchen shelf.
That's the surprise of these songs.
Awakening shows up in a mortar, a patched robe, a pot of herbs, the daily stuff of a woman's hands. And notice who's talking.

teach.h: OVER AND OVER, THEY SAY I.
teach.b: Over and over, the poems say I. I was a wife. I was worn out.
I went forth. I am free. They aren't stories told about women by someone else.
Each one is her voice, telling her own way out, in the words of her own life. Some of the sisters became teachers, and tomorrow brings one of them.

how: The Therigatha is part of the Pali Canon; Buddhists read and chant its verses, and it is valued as a record of women on the path telling their own stories.

games.why: the first sisters' songs are built from kitchen things: a mortar, a pestle, herbs dried in a pot. Mutta's freedom has the shape of her daily work.

practice: Tap the table once with your knuckle, like a pestle coming down, and listen until the sound is completely gone.
Then rest both hands flat and still, like tools set down when the work is finished, and sit with that stillness in your palms.
